1.q: ה֣וֹי שׁוֹדֵ֗ד וְ⁠אַתָּה֙ לֹ֣א שָׁד֔וּד וּ⁠בוֹגֵ֖ד וְ⁠לֹא בָ֣גְדוּ ב֑⁠וֹ כַּ⁠הֲתִֽמְ⁠ךָ֤ שׁוֹדֵד֙ תּוּשַּׁ֔ד כַּ⁠נְּלֹתְ⁠ךָ֥ לִ⁠בְגֹּ֖ד יִבְגְּדוּ בָֽ⁠ךְ
1.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [Woe to you, destroyer and betrayer, whom no one has yet destroyed or betrayed! When you stop your destroying and betraying, you yourself will be destroyed and betrayed]

Isaiah is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling, a pronouncement of grief and judgment against the destroyer. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [How terrible it will be for you]

The destruction described here does not happen immediately but at a future time, **When you finish destroying**. Your language may have a connecting phrase that you can use to show this. Alternate translation: [After you finish destroying]

The expression **you have not been destroyed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and no one has yet destroyed you]

The pronoun **they** does not refer to a specific group of people but is used in a general sense to refer to those who might betray the destroyer. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and people have not betrayed him]

The expression **you will be destroyed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [others will destroy you]

The pronoun **they** does not refer to a specific group of people but is used in a general sense to refer to those who will betray the destroyer. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [others will betray you]

2.note: This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [please be gracious to us]
By **us**, Isaiah means himself and the people of Judah but not Yahweh to whom he is speaking, so use the exclusive form of that word in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

Isaiah is speaking as if Yahweh’s help and support for his people were Yahweh being **their arm**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Be their strength and support]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please be their strength]
The pronoun **their** refers to the people of Judah. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the arm of the people of Judah]

By **our**, Isaiah means himself and the people of Judah but not Yahweh to whom he is speaking, so use the exclusive form of that word in your translation if your language marks that distinction. Alternate translation: [the salvation of your people]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [our savior]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **trouble**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [our suffering]

3.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **tumult**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [At the sound of loud shouting]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **exaltation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [when you exalt yourself]

4.note: The expression **your spoil will be gathered** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And your enemies will gather your spoil]
The word **your** is plural because Isaiah is addressing Judah’s enemies, so use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

The point of this comparison is that just as **the gathering of the caterpillar** is thorough and consuming, so is the way the spoil will be collected. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [And your spoil will be completely gathered, just as caterpillars consume everything]

Isaiah is using the possessive form to describe a **the gathering** of food that is performed by **the caterpillar**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [like caterpillars gathering their food]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the rushing of locusts** is swift and overwhelming, so is the way people rush upon the spoil. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [people rush upon it swiftly and overwhelm it]

Isaiah is using the possessive form to describe a **rushing** that is performed by **locusts**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [like locusts rushing]
The pronoun **it** refers to the spoil of the enemy. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [upon the spoil]

5.note: The expression **Yahweh is exalted** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Yahweh exalts himself]

The word translated as **for** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [Yahweh is exalted because]

Isaiah is speaking as if Yahweh’s supreme authority were his physically living in a high place. The ULT says **he inhabits the height**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he rules from his high position above all]

The terms **justice** and **righteousness** mean similar things. Isaiah is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [with complete fairness]
If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **justice** and **righteousness**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [with what is just and right]

6.note: Isaiah is speaking as if Yahweh were a firm foundation that provides **the stability of your times**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And he will keep you secure throughout your times]

Isaiah is using the possessive form to describe a **stability** that characterizes **your times**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [stability in your lifetimes]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **stability**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what secures]

Isaiah is speaking as if salvation, wisdom, and knowledge were a **wealth** of valuable possessions. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he will save them, make them wise, and give them knowledge, enriching them]

Isaiah is using the possessive form to describe a **wealth** that consists of **salvation, wisdom, and knowledge**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a rich source of salvation, wisdom, and knowledge] or [enriching them with salvation, wisdom, and knowledge]
If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **salvation, wisdom, and knowledge**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [being saved]

Isaiah is speaking as if **The fear of Yahweh** were **his treasure**, his most valuable possession. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The fear of Yahweh is his most valuable possession]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **fear**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [The reverence that people have for Yahweh]

Isaiah is using the possessive form to describe a **fear** that is directed toward **Yahweh**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Reverence for Yahweh]

7.note: Isaiah is using the term **Behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Look]

The pronoun **their** refers to the people of Judah and Jerusalem, whom Isaiah has been describing throughout this passage. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Judah’s warriors]

Isaiah is using the possessive form to describe **messengers** who are sent to negotiate **peace**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the messengers who were sent to negotiate peace]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **peace**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a truce]

8.note: The expression **The highways are deserted** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [No one travels the highways]

Isaiah is using the possessive form to describe a **traveler** who travels on **the road**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the traveler who travels on the road]
The pronoun **He** refers to the enemy, that is, Assyria. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Assyria has broken]

Some ancient manuscripts read “cities.” The ULT follows that reading. Other ancient manuscripts read “witnesses.” If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT. Alternate translation: [witnesses]

Although the term **man** is masculine, Isaiah is using the word in a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a phrase that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [he does not regard anyone]

9.note: Isaiah speaks of the land as if it were a living thing that could **mourn** and be **enfeebled**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The land has become barren and withered]

The expression **it is enfeebled** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [it grows weak]

Isaiah speaks of **Lebanon** as if it were a living thing that could display disgrace and wither. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Lebanon is not producing trees; they go wild]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **disgrace**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [is put to shame]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the Arabah** is dry and barren, so fertile **Sharon** has become desolate. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [Sharon has become as dry and barren as the Arabah]

Isaiah speaks of **Bashan** and **Carmel** as if they were living things that could be **shaking off** their foliage. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and Bashan and Carmel are losing their foliage]

Isaiah assumes that readers will know that Bashan and Carmel are very fertile areas. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and Bashan and Carmel are losing their foliage]

10.note: Yahweh is using **I will arise** as a common expression of the culture to indicate that he is about to begin taking action. He does not mean that he is getting out of bed or standing up from a seated position. If this expression does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Now I will begin to act]

The terms **exalt myself** and **lift myself up** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [I will greatly exalt myself]

11.note: Yahweh is speaking as if the enemy’s futile plans were a pregnancy that produces only **chaff** and **stubble**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You will conceive worthless things, you will bear what is useless]

11.q: תַּהֲר֥וּ חֲשַׁ֖שׁ תֵּ֣לְדוּ קַ֑שׁ רוּחֲ⁠כֶ֕ם אֵ֖שׁ תֹּאכַלְ⁠כֶֽם
11.note: The words **you** and **your** in this verse are plural because Yahweh is addressing Judah’s enemies, so use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.
The pronoun **You** refers to the enemy nation. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [You, the enemy nation, will conceive]
The pronoun **your** refers to the enemy nation. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the breath of your people]

Yahweh is speaking as if the enemy’s own hostility were a **breath** and **a fire** that would consume them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your own anger will consume you]

12.note: Yahweh is speaking as if the defeated peoples would be **burnings of lime**, completely consumed. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And peoples will be completely burned up] or [And peoples will be totally consumed by fire]

Yahweh is speaking as if the enemies were **thorns** that would be **cut down** and would **burn in fire**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the enemies will be burned like trash]

Yahweh is leaving out one or more words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You could supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [like thorns that are cut down, they will burn in fire]

The expression **thorns cut down** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [thorns that someone cuts down]

13.q: שִׁמְע֥וּ רְחוֹקִ֖ים אֲשֶׁ֣ר עָשִׂ֑יתִי וּ⁠דְע֥וּ קְרוֹבִ֖ים גְּבֻרָתִֽ⁠י
13.note: Yahweh is using the two extremes of **the faraway** and **the near** together to mean everyone everywhere. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Hear, all people, both far and near, what I have done, and know, all of you, my might]

Yahweh is using the plural adjective **faraway** as a noun to mean a certain kind of people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [those who are far away]

Yahweh is using the plural adjective **near** as a noun to mean a certain kind of people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [those who are nearby]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe **might** that belongs to him. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how mighty I am]

14.note: Isaiah speaks of **trembling** as if it were a living thing that could **seize** people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the godless shake with fear]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **trembling**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the godless tremble greatly]

Isaiah is using the adjective **godless** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [those who are godless]
By **us**, the sinners mean themselves but not those outside their group, so use the exclusive form of that word in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

14.q: מִ֣י יָג֣וּר לָ֗⁠נוּ אֵ֚שׁ אוֹכֵלָ֔ה מִי־יָג֥וּר לָ֖⁠נוּ מוֹקְדֵ֥י עוֹלָֽם
14.note: The sinners are using the question form to emphasize that no one can endure God’s judgment. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [None of us can sojourn {with} a devouring fire! None of us can sojourn with burnings of eternity!]

14.q: מִ֣י יָג֣וּר לָ֗⁠נוּ אֵ֚שׁ אוֹכֵלָ֔ה מִי־יָג֥וּר לָ֖⁠נוּ מוֹקְדֵ֥י עוֹלָֽם
14.note: The sinners are speaking as if God’s judgment were a **devouring fire** and **burnings of eternity**, meaning something that completely consumes and never stops. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Who among us can sojourn with God’s consuming judgment? Who among us can sojourn with his never-ending destruction?]

The sinners are using the question form to emphasize that no one can endure God’s eternal judgment. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [None of us can sojourn with burnings of eternity!]

Isaiah is using the possessive form to describe **burnings** that are characterized by being of **eternity**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [{with} eternal burnings]

15.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousnesses**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [righteously]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **uprightnesses**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [things that are upright]

Isaiah is using the possessive form to describe **gain** that comes from **oppressions**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the gain that comes from oppressing others]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **oppressions**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [oppressing others]

Isaiah is using **the one shaking his palms from taking hold of a bribe** as a common expression of the culture to mean “the person who refuses to accept a bribe.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the one who refuses to accept a bribe]

Isaiah is speaking as if a righteous person would literally be **stopping** or blocking up his **ear** so that he could not hear about **bloodshed**. He means that such a person does not even consider acting violently. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the one who will not even consider acting violently]

Isaiah is speaking as if a righteous person would literally be **shutting** his **eyes** so that he could not see anything **evil**. He means that such a person does not even consider doing something wicked. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the one who will not even consider doing something wicked]

16.note: The pronoun **he** refers to the person described in the previous verse who walks in righteousness and speaks what is upright. The pronoun is repeated for emphasis. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the one who walks in righteousness, he will stay]

Isaiah is speaking as if the safety God provides for the righteous person were literally enabling him to **stay on the heights**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [this person, he will be kept safe]

Isaiah is using the possessive form to describe **strongholds** that are located on **cliffs**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [strongholds on the cliffs]

Isaiah is speaking as if God’s protection of the righteous person were **strongholds of cliffs** serving as **his refuge**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he will be well protected]

The expression **His bread is given** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [God will provide his bread]

The expression **his waters are secured** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [his waters will not run dry]

17.note: Here and throughout verses 17-20, the words “you” and “your” are singular because they refer to a representative Judean person of the type Isaiah describes in verses 15–16. (Such a person shuts his eyes so as not to look on evil. Isaiah describes here the wonderful things that he will see instead.) So use singular forms in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

Isaiah is using **Your eyes** to represent Judea, who will see. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You will see the king]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **beauty**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [looking beautiful]

Isaiah is speaking as if the king’s vast domain were **a land of distances** stretching far in every direction. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a vast land]

18.note: Isaiah is speaking as if a person’s thoughts were located in his **heart**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Your thoughts will focus]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **terror**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [on terrifying things]

Isaiah is using the question form to emphasize that the oppressor who once weighed tribute is now gone. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [The one weighing is no longer there.]

18.q: אַיֵּ֤ה סֹפֵר֙ אַיֵּ֣ה שֹׁקֵ֔ל אַיֵּ֖ה סֹפֵ֥ר אֶת־הַ⁠מִּגְדָּלִֽים
18.note: Isaiah is using the question form to emphasize that the enemy officer who once counted towers is now gone. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [The one counting is gone! The one weighing is gone! The one counting towers is gone!]

19.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **arrogance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [acting arrogantly]

Here, **lip** represents “language” or “speech.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [of speech too difficult to understand]

Isaiah is using the possessive form to describe speech that is characterized by being **deep**, that is, incomprehensible. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [too obscure in speech]
Here, **tongue** represents “language” or “speech.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [stammering of speech]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **understanding**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [one can understand]

20.note: The word translated as **Gaze** is an imperative, but it communicates a condition rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a condition for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a condition. Alternate translation: [When you gaze at Zion]
By **our**, Isaiah means himself and the people of Judah but not those outside their community, so use the exclusive form of that word in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

Isaiah is using **Your eyes** to represent the whole person who will see. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You will see Jerusalem]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **habitation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a place where people can securely live]

Isaiah is speaking as if Jerusalem were **a tent** that would never be taken down, meaning it is a permanent and secure dwelling place. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a permanent home that will never be dismantled]
The word **one** is used in a general sense to mean that no person will take the tent down. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [no one will take it down]

The expression **all of its cords will not be broken** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and no one will break any of its cords]

The word **one** is used in a general sense to mean that no person will pull up the stakes. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [its stakes will never be pulled up]

21.note: Isaiah uses the word **Instead** here to indicate a contrast between the insecurity of the tent in the previous verse and the mighty presence of Yahweh. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [But]
By **us**, Isaiah means himself and the people of Judah but not those outside their community, so use the exclusive form of that word in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

Isaiah is speaking as if Yahweh’s protective presence were **a place of rivers, streams, broad of hands**. By this he means that Yahweh’s presence provides security like a wide river that enemy ships cannot cross. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a place protected by wide rivers and streams]

Isaiah is using the possessive form to describe a **place** that is characterized by having wide **rivers** and **streams**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a place with rivers]

Isaiah is using **broad of hands** as a common expression of the culture to mean “wide” or “expansive.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a place with wide rivers and streams]

Isaiah is using the possessive form to describe a **ship** that is propelled by **oar**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [A ship propelled by oars]

21.q: בַּל־תֵּ֤לֶךְ בּ⁠וֹ֙ אֳנִי־שַׁ֔יִט וְ⁠צִ֥י אַדִּ֖יר לֹ֥א יַעַבְרֶֽ⁠נּוּ
21.note: The pronoun **it** refers to the river described earlier in this verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [A ship propelled by oars will not go on the river and no mighty vessel will pass over the river]

22.note: The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is because]

22.q: יְהוָה֙ שֹׁפְטֵ֔⁠נוּ יְהוָ֖ה מְחֹקְקֵ֑⁠נוּ יְהוָ֥ה מַלְכֵּ֖⁠נוּ
22.note: By **our**, Isaiah means himself and the people of Judah but not those outside their community, so use the exclusive form of that word in your translation if your language marks that distinction. Alternate translation: [Yahweh is the judge, lawgiver and king of his people]
The pronoun **He** refers to Yahweh. Isaiah repeats the pronoun for emphasis. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh himself will save us]

23.q: נִטְּשׁ֖וּ חֲבָלָ֑יִ⁠ךְ בַּל יְחַזְּק֤וּ כֵן תָּרְנָ⁠ם֙ בַּל פָּ֣רְשׂוּ נֵ֔ס
23.note: Isaiah is speaking as if the enemy nation were a **ship** whose ropes are loosened and whose mast cannot be secured and whose sail cannot be spread, meaning the enemy is powerless and defeated. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Your strength is gone; you cannot stand firm; you cannot advance]

The expression **Your ropes are loosened** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Your ropes have come loose]
The pronoun **Your** refers to the enemy nation, which Isaiah is now addressing directly. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The enemy nation’s ropes]
The pronoun **they** refers to the ropes of the ship. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the ropes do not hold]

Isaiah is using the possessive form to describe **booty** that consists of **spoil**, that is, plundered goods. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [much booty and spoil]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **abundance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in heaps]
This is poetic language. Isaiah uses a verb and its related noun together for emphasis. If your language has a way to express this kind of emphasis, you could use it here. See the UST.

Isaiah is using the adjective **lame** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [lame people]

The expression **spoil in abundance is divided** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [spoil in abundance that they divide]

24.note: Isaiah is speaking as if the people’s suffering and distress were a physical illness. The ULT says **I am sick**, using sickness as a metaphor for distress. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I am suffering]

The expression **forgiven of iniquity** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [will receive Yahweh’s forgiveness for their iniquity]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **iniquity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the wrong they have done]
